structural_agency.definition: Structural agency is the user's "ability to navigate and shape complex systems and institutions." It concerns meaningful action to shape one's conditions in the world, mediated by social, cultural, technical, and institutional forces. It is not merely task completion, cognitive clarity, emotional reassurance, interpersonal support, or a feeling of being more capable. It requires that the user is seeking practical capacity in relation to structures that organize rules, resources, expertise, authority, opportunities, constraints, or consequential decisions.
purposes: Understanding how a consequential system, institution, process, rule, or decision structure works.
Translating specialized, formal, expert, or institutional language into actionable understanding.
Deciding how to proceed in a situation shaped by rules, constraints, eligibility requirements, authority, unequal information, or asymmetric power.
Preparing to access consequential resources, services, opportunities, rights, protections, credentials, remedies, or forms of support.
Planning concrete steps, communications, documentation, applications, negotiations, complaints, or other actions directed at a real-world system or institution.

Contesting, challenging, negotiating, or protecting oneself or others against consequential decisions, organizational power, material pressure, exposure, exclusion, mistreatment, or administrative complexity.
Building durable capacity to handle future shocks, disruptions, risks, or system-imposed constraints.

domains.title: Workplace and Professional Practice
domains.scope: Real-world situations where the user is DOING THEIR JOB as an employee or professional inside an organization: workplace communications with managers, HR, colleagues, clients, or counterparties; operations, logistics, and resource planning; designing or improving organizational processes and procedures; producing professional or technical documentation required by their role; and making the internal business case for a decision. The defining feature is the user acting within their organization's structures to carry out, improve, or navigate their work. It does not include getting hired, running one's own venture for income, or legal disputes over workplace rights.

domains.title: Generating Business Income
domains.scope: Conversations where the user's OWN earning or venture is the active object: starting/structuring/running a business, freelancing, self-employment, monetizing a creative output/platform/audience, acquiring and retaining paying customers/clients, pricing/quoting/invoicing and getting paid, dealing with vendors/suppliers/marketplaces/seller platforms, buying property as a rental/landlord income venture, fundraising for a for-profit venture, or advancing one's own earnings from labor (compensation negotiation: salary/rate/raise/offer/equity). The defining feature is the user acting to generate, grow, or protect income from an enterprise or from selling their own work/labor, navigating the market, platform, client, and commercial systems that govern getting paid. Mere mention of 'business' or 'startup' does not qualify; the user's own earning must be the actual object of action.

domains.title: Employment and Career Advancement
domains.scope: Real-world situations where the user is trying to GET HIRED or advance their own career as an employee or professional: searching and applying for jobs, resumes/CVs and cover letters, job applications and supplementary questions, interview preparation, career planning and transitions, acquiring skills or courses specifically to become employable in a role, professional networking, and academic-career advancement (fellowship or publication submissions). The defining feature is the user acting on the hiring or career system to obtain or advance employment. It does not include running one's own business or venture, negotiating pay as income strategy, or asserting legal workplace rights.

domains.title: Obtaining Legal Advice
domains.scope: Conversations where the user's own real-world situation turns on law, legal rights/obligations, or a formal legal/quasi-legal process: contracts, compliance, IP/licensing, regulations; courts, claims, disputes, hearings, citations/tickets, appeals, complaints, legal/police records; immigration & citizenship (visas, residency, work permits, asylum, naturalization, immigration forms/eligibility/procedures, immigration appeals); employment RIGHTS (wrongful termination, unpaid wages, discrimination, harassment, protected leave, accommodations as a rights dispute, severance/non-compete legal review, labor-board filings); and family & estate legal processes (custody, divorce, child/spousal support, prenup, wills, trusts, probate, inheritance process, guardianship, power of attorney). In-domain means the user's own situation is governed by these legal frameworks or processes; it does NOT require that the conversation be structural agency.

domains.title: Obtaining Education
domains.scope: Real-world situations where a person is navigating, accessing, or acting within formal education systems and institutions: K-12 schools, colleges/universities, graduate and professional programs, vocational/certificate/credential programs, and the bureaucratic processes attached to them (admissions, enrollment, registration, transfer/articulation, dual-enrollment, financial aid/scholarships, tuition payment plans with the school, disability accommodations, grading/transcripts, degree/certification requirements, academic standing/discipline, and student/parent interaction with school authorities). The user is a student, applicant, prospective student, parent/guardian, or educator/staff acting on their own behalf within these institutions.

domains.title: Help with Consumer Finances and/or Taxes
domains.scope: Conversations where the user's real-world situation centers on managing, protecting, or making decisions about their own (or their household's) personal money and the financial-administrative systems attached to it: budgeting, banking, debt, credit, loans, savings, personal investing/retirement, consumer purchases/refunds/warranties/chargebacks, AND personal taxes, insurance, claims, benefits eligibility, coverage, premiums, and deductions. The defining axis is the user as a consumer/taxpayer/policyholder navigating money systems and financial bureaucracy that shape their personal financial position — distinct from earning income/revenue and distinct from the underlying need a financial product covers. Property tax, capital gains on a home sale, and homeowner/renter insurance are always in this domain even when a dwelling is involved.

domains.title: Obtaining Housing
domains.scope: The user's real-world situation concerns getting, keeping, paying for, fixing, leaving, or living in a specific physical dwelling, and navigating the systems attached to where they live: rental tenancy (landlord/tenant), home buying/selling to live in, mortgages as a means of obtaining/keeping a home, moving, evictions short of litigation, repairs/habitability, utilities tied to the dwelling (water/gas/electric/internet hookups, billing disputes, shutoffs), property/zoning/planning/permits for one's own dwelling or property, homeowner/condo/HOA matters, finding/affording a residential care facility as a place to live, and individual navigation of local public services or infrastructure tied to where one lives (transit access for getting around one's area, municipal services). domains.title: Navigating Healthcare Systems

AI-driven solutions can complement traditional approaches to improve mental health outcomes, enhance access to care, and empower individuals with mental health concerns.

Understanding the Challenges in Mental Health

Mental health disorders affect millions of people globally, yet many face barriers to accessing timely and effective care. These barriers include stigma, lack of resources, and shortage of mental health professionals.

How AI Can Revolutionize Mental Health Initiatives

  • Early Diagnosis and Screening: AI algorithms can analyze vast amounts of data to identify individuals at risk for mental health disorders, enabling early intervention and support.
  • Personalized Treatment Plans: AI can tailor treatment plans to individual needs by considering factors such as symptoms, medical history, and lifestyle.
  • Remote and Scalable Care: AI-powered telemedicine platforms and chatbots provide convenient and accessible mental health support, especially for those in remote or underserved areas.
  • Symptom Tracking and Self-Management: AI-enabled apps can help individuals track their symptoms, engage in self-care activities, and monitor their progress over time.
  • Empowerment and Support: AI chatbots and virtual assistants offer emotional support, coping mechanisms, and guidance for managing mental health challenges.

Benefits of AI in Mental Health Care

  • Improved Access to Care: AI expands the reach of mental health services, making it available to individuals who may not have otherwise sought help.
  • Cost-Effectiveness: AI-driven solutions can reduce healthcare costs by promoting early intervention and reducing the need for expensive hospitalizations.
  • Enhanced Treatment Outcomes: AI can personalize treatments and provide ongoing support, leading to better outcomes for individuals with mental health disorders.
  • Stigma Reduction: AI-powered anonymous platforms and chatbots can encourage individuals to seek help without fear of judgment.
  • Empowerment and Resilience: AI tools empower individuals to manage their mental health and build coping mechanisms.

Considerations for Ethical and Responsible Use

  • Data Privacy and Security: AI systems rely on sensitive personal data. Ensuring privacy and security measures is crucial to prevent data breaches.
  • Algorithmic Bias: AI algorithms must be trained on diverse data sets to avoid perpetuating biases that could impact access to care and treatment outcomes.
  • Human-Centric Approach: AI should complement and enhance human interactions, not replace them. Collaboration between AI and mental health professionals is essential.
  • Transparency and Accountability: The development and use of AI in mental health should be transparent and accountable, with clear explanations of algorithms and decision-making processes.

Conclusion

AI holds immense potential to revolutionize mental health initiatives. By addressing barriers to care, personalizing treatments, and empowering individuals, AI can significantly improve mental health outcomes and well-being. However, ethical and responsible use of AI is paramount to ensure equity, privacy, and transparency.

Inflation slows to 2.8% in Canada in June, within Bank of Canada's target range
Alicja Siekierska
Alicja Siekierska
Tue, July 18, 2023 at 8:33 a.m. GMT-4·3 min read
TORONTO ON-June 26.Gas prices surged back up above two dollars a litre in the GTA again after a week below the high water mark price.  (R.J. Johnston/Toronto Star)        (R.J. Johnston/Toronto Star via Getty Images)
Canada’s annual inflation rate slowed to 2.8 per cent in June. (R.J. Johnston/Toronto Star via Getty Images)
Canada’s annual inflation rate slowed to 2.8 per cent in June, according to Statistics Canada, but Canadians continue to face price pressures as rising food prices and mortgage interest costs push ever higher.

The rise in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) was down from a 3.4 per cent increase in May, and brings it in line with the Bank of Canada's previous forecast that inflation would ease to around 3 per cent by mid-year. It marks the first time in 27 months that annual headline inflation was within the central bank's target range of between one and three per cent.

On a monthly basis, CPI increased 0.1 per cent in June. Seasonally adjusted, the increase was also 0.1 per cent.

Base-year effects in gasoline prices drove the slowdown in CPI, with prices falling 21.6 per cent year-over-year. Statistics Canada said the annual decrease was a result of elevated prices last year as China started to ease some COVID-19 health restrictions. On a monthly basis, Canadians paid 1.9 per cent more for gas than they did in May.

Food prices continue to push stubbornly higher and remain one of the largest contributors to inflation, Statistics Canada said. The cost of food purchased from grocery stores increased 9.1 per cent annually in June, up from 9 per cent in May. The biggest contributors to the increase in food prices were the cost of meat (up 6.9 per cent), bakery products (up 12.9 per cent), dairy products (up 7.4 per cent) and other food preparations (up 10.2 per cent). The cost of fresh fruit jumped 10.4 per cent, in part because of a 30 per cent month-over-month increase in grape prices.

But Canadians did see some price relief in June, with Statistic Canada calling the deceleration "fairly broad-based." Cell phone prices fell 14.7 per cent annually in June, following an 8.2 per cent annual decline in May. Internet prices also dropped 3.2 per cent annually in June, after rising 1 per cent annually in May.

The slowdown in inflation comes shortly after the Bank of Canada hiked its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point, bringing it to 5 per cent. But the central bank predicted it will take even longer for inflation to return to 2 per cent.

Royce Mendes, managing director and head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said shortly after the release Tuesday that while inflation has fallen into the central bank's target range "there are signs pointing to slower progress from this point on."

"The Bank of Canada’s preferred measures of core inflation, which exclude significant moves in individual categories, shows that underlying price pressures remain sticky," he wrote in a research note.

"There’s scope for headline inflation to reaccelerate in the months to come as some of the recent progress can be chalked up to one-off moves lower in prices."

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg had expected inflation to fall to 3 per cent year-over-year in June.

How to design a reliable and secure backup plan.

Database configuration settings that affect performance.

RESIDENT, NON-DOMICILED COMPANIES
The scope of taxation in Malta depends on the person’s residence and domicile. In the Income Tax Act, a ‘person’ is defined as an individual and a body of persons which includes companies, any fellowship, society or other association of persons, whether corporate or unincorporated and whether vested with legal personality.

While the term ‘domicile’ is not defined in the Income Tax Acts, in the case of a body of persons, it is deemed to be the place of incorporation or principal seat of registration of the body of persons. A company which is registered in Malta is deemed to be domiciled and tax resident in Malta from the date of its incorporation, and is subject to a flat rate of 35% on its worldwide income[1]. This does not mean, however, that a Maltese company which operates abroad may never be taxed in that country. Cases of dual residence may arise, for instance when one State attaches importance to the place of incorporation whereas another attaches importance to the place of effective management.

A company incorporated outside of Malta is considered to be resident in Malta only if its place of effective management and control is in Malta. As a general rule, ‘the place of effective management’ is defined as the place where the key management and commercial decisions that are necessary for the conduct of the company’s business are in substance made. This is generally, though not necessarily, the place where the board of directors meet and resolve business.

Therefore, a company which is incorporated in Malta is considered to be resident and domiciled in Malta, while a company which is incorporated outside Malta but has its control and management in Malta will be considered as resident but not domiciled in Malta.

Companies which are resident but not domiciled (or vice versa) in Malta are subject to tax in Malta on all income and chargeable gains arising in Malta, and on income arising outside Malta which is remitted back to Malta. No tax is payable on foreign income which is not received in Malta and on capital gains arising outside Malta to a company which is not ordinarily resident and domiciled in Malta, even if remitted to Malta. On the other hand, companies which are neither incorporated nor resident in Malta are only chargeable on income and capital gains arising in Malta.

A company registered abroad that shifts its management and control seat to Malta is deemed to be resident, but not domiciled, in Malta and would be able to reap the fiscal advantages available to Malta resident companies. Such advantages include the application of the tax credit imputation mechanism and the tax refunds available to the shareholders of the company on a final distribution of dividends. These fiscal advantages are discussed further below.

Malta resident companies (even those not domiciled) are to allocate distributable profits to one or more of 5 tax accounts, depending on the nature and the source of the profits. These tax accounts are: the Foreign Income Account (FIA), the Maltese Taxed Account (MTA), the Final Tax Account (FTA), the Immovable Property Account (IPA), and the Untaxed Account (UA).

Full imputation system
Malta operates a full imputation system for dividends paid out from the prof­its of the company. Dividends are subject to tax in the hands of the shareholder however, shareholders receive a full imputation credit for the tax paid by the company. The full imputation system ensures that the shareholder is not subject to further tax on dividends distributed and therefore, eliminates economic double taxation.

Tax Refunds
Furthermore, the effective tax paid may be reduced through the application of various refunds available to the shareholders of a Malta resident company. Although often associated with the imputation system, the tax refund is over and above the imputation credit outlined above and is intended to reduce overall tax burden in Malta in the hands of the shareholder.

Available Tax Refunds in Malta:
100% Refund – Applies when profits are derived from a participating holding which qualifies for the participation exemption.
6/7ths Refund – This type of refund is generally due on those profits earned from trading activities. Taking into account such refund, the effective rate of tax works out at 5%.
5/7ths Refund – This type of refund is generally due in respect of income derived from passive interest and royalties and income from participating holdings which do not qualify for the participation exemption. The effect rate of tax works out at 10%.
2/3rds Refund – Available in those instances where the company has claimed double taxation relief. The refund depends on the type of double taxation relief availed of and is limited to the tax paid in Malta.
The participation exemption (or 100% refund) mentioned above applies to a Malta registered company which derives profits or gains from a participating holding in a non-resident entity. In such a case, the Malta holding company may decide:

either to apply an outright exemption from tax or
to include such income or gains as part of the taxable income of the Malta resident company and pay tax at the default rate of 35%. Following the distribution of dividends by the Malta resident company out of the said income or gains, the recipient shareholders would be entitled to a full (100%) refund of the tax paid by the company on such income or gains.
Withholding tax
Malta does not levy withholding tax on distributions of dividends to non-resident shareholders. Moreover, as long as certain conditions are met, Malta would not levy any withholding tax on payments of interest and royalties to persons not resident in Malta.

Worldwide basis of taxation is not applicable to companies who are resident but not domiciled in Malta;
No tax is payable on foreign income which is not remitted to Malta
Capital gains remitted to Malta are not subject to any tax whatsoever;
